https://euobserver.com/232638/cracks-but.text: When a totalitarian regime topples, the first signs can seem trivial. Someone says the unsayable. It may be a small voice or a quiet one. But it punctures the climate of fear. The authorities look stupid if they respond, weak if they don’t. Taboos shrivel. Plots mushroom. Power evaporates. I witnessed that in the then Czechoslovakia in 1989. There are hints of something similar in Russia now, with the remarks that became public last week by Andrei Klepach, chief economist of the state-run VEB bank. Russia is awash with unsayable truths, held back by complicity and repression. Klepach breached that wall when he spoke to the Nikitsky Club , an upmarket Moscow discussion club. He said that western support for Ukraine made the war of attrition unwinnable. The idea that Ukraine would collapse was an “illusion”; meanwhile Russia was becoming a backward country and a social crisis was brewing. Echoes of the 1989 Velvet Revolution? My mind went back to August 1989, when I was scouring the news kiosks of Prague in search of an obscure management journal published by a communist-controlled research institute specialising in agricultural economics. But that August every copy of the normally deathly-dull Technický Magazin , had sold out. It carried an article called “Forecasting and Reconstruction” that laid bare the failure of the planned economy, which was making Czechoslovakia, the author wrote, into a backward country. This was true. Everyone knew it. Backwardness was humiliating for people who knew that before the socialist miracle, their country had been the industrial heartland of central Europe. Samizdat papers and foreign radio stations said it. The media in other fast-reforming communist countries (Poland, Hungary, even the Soviet Union) said it. But the official line in Czechoslovakia, rigorously enforced by the regime installed by the Soviet-led invasion of 1968, was that reform was unnecessary. The article’s author was a little-known economist called Miloš Zeman. He was told to go on state-controlled television and backtrack. Instead he repeated his message. That programme went out too (another interesting failure of censorship). He was sacked. The fire-breathing Communist Party daily Rudé Právo [Red Justice] denounced him. He sued for a right of reply: a move that would have seemed absurd only months earlier. Before the case went to court, the regime had collapsed in what later became known as the Velvet Revolution. The parallels are not exact. Read more Putin has become a prisoner of his own war The Kremlin in 1989 was visibly impatient with the boneheaded bureaucrats of Prague, and behind the scenes was searching for a more forward-looking leadership: something Zeman was keen to note at the time.
